How to use this

HomeWhat to stay away from

!Stay away from these

35 warnings from your videos, worst first inside each group. Each one says why, and what to do instead.

Don't burn money

Tokens, models and subscriptions: the bill comes from where work is sent and how much context rides along.

  • Stay away
    Don't send every job to a top-tier model

    Why: Moe Lueker routes each task to the cheapest capable model and keeps Opus and Fable for hard work. Alex Finn puts his own Claude Opus use at about 40 US dollars a day.

    Do this instead: Use a cheap main model for routine work and escalate to a stronger one only when needed; Simon Scrapes's /advisor shows the pattern.

    Said by Moe Lueker, Alex Finn, Simon Scrapes

    Video 1Video 2Video 3
  • Stay away
    Don't run an agent without a spend limit on its key

    Why: Jack Roberts and Metics Media both point to OpenRouter's spend limits, which can be set per key, so one runaway agent cannot drain the shared budget.

    Do this instead: Give each agent its own OpenRouter key with its own limit.

    Said by Jack Roberts, Metics Media

    Video 1Video 2
  • Be careful
    Don't bill a model for jobs that are just a script

    Why: Python Simplified shows a Hermes cron job with a no-agent checkbox that runs the script and never calls the model, and an auxiliary model setting that sends background work to a free OpenRouter model.

    Do this instead: Tick no-agent for script-only cron jobs and set a cheap auxiliary model.

    Said by Python Simplified

    Video 1
  • Be careful
    Don't leave old cron jobs running

    Why: Alex Finn says pruning and pausing old cron jobs improves speed and cost.

    Do this instead: List each job's purpose, pause what nobody reads, and archive rather than delete.

    Said by Alex Finn

    Video 1Video 2
  • Be careful
    Don't trust a repo's token-saving claim

    Why: Caveman claims about 65 per cent fewer output tokens, but Nate Herk's own test found about 8.5 per cent, and he measured no saving from RTK. The codebase-memory claim of 99 per cent comes from Sharbel A. repeating the project.

    Do this instead: Measure on one agent for a week before it becomes a fleet rule.

    Said by Nate Herk, Sharbel A., Teku AI

    Video 1Video 2Video 3
  • Be careful
    Don't let context pile up or break the cache

    Why: Sharbel A. explains that history is re-sent every turn, and that changing model, effort, MCP or plugin toggles, or compacting, resets the prompt cache and costs more. Jay E of RoboNuggets shows Cache Tax, which warns before a send once the cache has gone cold.

    Do this instead: One session per topic, start fresh with /new when context fills, and avoid mid-session toggles.

    Said by Sharbel A., Greg Isenberg and Alex Finn, Jay E

    Video 1Video 2Video 3
  • Be careful
    Don't leave unused skills, tools and MCP servers loaded

    Why: Greg Isenberg's guest says switching off some of Hermes's roughly 150 built-in skills saves cost. Sharbel A. says to turn off unused MCP servers, and Wanderloots prunes each bot's tool toggles to stop tool loops.

    Do this instead: Audit each agent's skills, toolsets and MCP list and keep only what its lane uses.

    Said by Alex Finn, Sharbel A., Wanderloots

    Video 1Video 2Video 3

Don't fall for the hype

Workflow traps: too many agents, borrowed benchmarks, paywalled freebies and promises of easy money.

  • Be careful
    Don't spin up agents without lanes

    Why: Dan Martell's AGENT framework gives each agent one lane, a one-sentence definition of done and more freedom only as it earns it, and his Rule of R asks whether a task is repetitive, rules-based and worth the time.

    Do this instead: Write each agent's lane and done-test before adding another.

    Said by Dan Martell

    Video 1
  • Be careful
    Don't let agents chat without a turn cap

    Why: Wanderloots caps turns in a shared room so a human must step in. Jack Roberts says a Hermes goal has a 20-turn budget by default.

    Do this instead: Set a turn cap on every group room and goal, then decide as a human.

    Said by Wanderloots, Jack Roberts

    Video 1Video 2
  • Be careful
    Don't read star counts as a safety or quality rating

    Why: Nuno Tavares says to skip Scrapling even though it shows about 87,900 GitHub stars. Agent Reach shows about 101,300 and is praised by Teku AI. Stars were checked on 25 Oct 2026 and measure attention only.

    Do this instead: Review every skill whatever its stars, and log Sentinel's verdict in the vault.

    Said by Nuno Tavares, Teku AI

    Video 1Video 2
  • Minor
    Don't add an orchestration layer before trying the native board

    Why: NetworkChuck loves Paperclip, which brings an org chart, secrets and routines of its own. Metics Media, Alex Finn and Tina Huang run multi-agent work on Hermes's built-in Kanban board.

    Do this instead: Try the native Kanban board first and add a meta layer only if it falls short.

    Said by NetworkChuck, Metics Media, Alex Finn

    Video 1Video 2Video 3
  • Minor
    Don't believe a free label until you see the paywall

    Why: Komputer Mechanic's free-prompts title leads to a $10-a-month membership. Mason Fitzgerald's RAG package, Julian Goldie's Agent OS and AI Labs's RTK skill sit behind paid communities.

    Do this instead: Check what is actually free before investing time, and copy the idea instead of buying the product.

    Said by Komputer Mechanic, Mason Fitzgerald, Julian Goldie, AI Labs

    Video 1Video 2Video 3Video 4
  • Minor
    Don't expect the agent to pay for itself

    Why: Dubibubi let an agent run a digital-product Etsy shop for 10 days and it made 4.55 dollars. The Next New Thing's pay-for-itself episode is a Zapier-sponsored roundup. The one lasting lesson was cutting tokens per listing from 4 per cent to 0.33 per cent of a weekly limit.

    Do this instead: Judge each agent by hours saved on a named task, not by promised income.

    Said by Dubibubi, The Next New Thing

    Video 1Video 2
  • Minor
    Don't switch models by a name from a caption

    Why: The reports are built from auto-generated captions and flag many model names as garbled; GPT-6 Astra came through as Chief 6 Astra, and Sol 5.6 is likely a mishearing. Several videos are sponsor-shaped, such as the Zapier and OpenAI segments.

    Do this instead: Confirm any model name against OpenRouter's model list before moving an agent.

    Said by Julian Goldie, Lead Gen Jay

    Video 1Video 2Video 3

Don't install these blindly

Skills, plugins and MCP servers are text and code someone else wrote; treat each one as untrusted until proven otherwise.

  • Stay away
    Don't install a skill from a pasted GitHub link or a public registry unread

    Why: Futurepedia shows skills going in by pasting a link, but Tina Huang avoids ClawHub skills unless the author is trusted, and Metics Media says to review anything from the Hermes Skills Hub before use.

    Do this instead: Have Sentinel read the skill file line by line first, and prefer authors you can name.

    Said by Tina Huang, Metics Media, Futurepedia

    Video 1Video 2Video 3Video 4
  • Stay away
    Don't assume a skill file is harmless text

    Why: A skill is instructions the agent obeys, so it can carry a hidden push. The Next New Thing reported a science skill that steers users to a paid product from inside its own skill file.

    Do this instead: Run a prompt-injection check before install: Jack Roberts demos Bouncer for Hermes, and Futurepedia shows Nvidia's Skill Inspector.

    Said by The Next New Thing, Jack Roberts, Futurepedia

    Video 1Video 2Video 3
  • Stay away
    Don't leave the Phone Harness plugin switched on in messaging channels

    Why: Julian Goldie says the community plugin is on by default in messaging apps, so anyone who can message your bot could drive the phone. The plugin's author is given only with low confidence in the report and no repo was named.

    Do this instead: Turn the phone tool off per platform with the hermes tools command, or skip the plugin.

    Said by Julian Goldie

    Video 1
  • Be careful
    Don't install Claude Mem or Context Mode because they are popular

    Why: Nate Herk tested over a hundred repos for Claude and says to skip Claude Mem because it sends data by default, and Context Mode because of a usage-limit bug.

    Do this instead: Test any memory or context plugin on a throwaway setup and read what it sends before it touches real data.

    Said by Nate Herk

    Video 1
  • Be careful
    Don't install tools that work by getting around site blockers

    Why: Nuno Tavares says to skip Scrapling, a free Firecrawl replacement, because it gets around blockers. Teku AI praises Agent Reach for getting past 403 bot blocks, which is the same trait.

    Do this instead: Use an approved scraper for research jobs and let Sentinel decide whether a bypass tool is acceptable at all.

    Said by Nuno Tavares, Teku AI

    Video 1Video 2Video 3
  • Be careful
    Don't load giant skill packs wholesale

    Why: The pick-lists name packs of 49 marketing skills, 292 skills in ECC, 279 role agents and 700+ skill files in Open Montage. AI Labs shows a retriever cutting skill context from about 11,000 to 2,300 tokens, which shows what an unfiltered pile costs.

    Do this instead: Install the one or two skills a given agent needs and switch off the rest.

    Said by Sharbel A., The Next New Thing, AI Edge, AI Labs

    Video 1Video 2Video 3Video 4
  • Minor
    Don't add a skill that already ships with Hermes or costs more than it earns

    Why: Teku AI calls Humanizer token heavy and Sharbel A. notes its skill file is 29.6 KB; a playlist-one note in the catalogue says it is already built into Hermes.

    Do this instead: Check the built-in list first, and use Simon Scrapes's test: run the job with and without the skill and keep it only if it helps.

    Said by Teku AI, Sharbel A., Simon Scrapes

    Video 1Video 2Video 3

Don't leave the server open

Security mistakes on a VPS full of agents: who can talk to them, what they can touch, and what faces the internet.

  • Stay away
    Don't open a bot to every user

    Why: Python Simplified shows that a single environment variable, TELEGRAM_ALLOW_ALL_USERS set to true, opens the bot to everyone, so anyone can chat with the agent.

    Do this instead: Restrict admin commands to your own ID in the Hermes config and check who the bot thinks you are.

    Said by Python Simplified

    Video 1
  • Stay away
    Don't paste API keys into chat

    Why: Jack Roberts says keys should never go into a conversation, where they linger in history. Chris's own no-secrets-in-Discord rule is the same idea.

    Do this instead: Set keys as environment variables; Lead Gen Jay keeps tokens in Doppler, a central store.

    Said by Jack Roberts, Lead Gen Jay

    Video 1Video 2Video 3
  • Stay away
    Don't give an agent broader access than its job needs

    Why: Nimrod gives agents scoped read-only keys in Jira, GitLab and GitHub, read-only database users that cannot see personal-data tables, and a small local MCP proxy exposing only allowed routes. Nate Herk says to make Supabase read-only.

    Do this instead: One scoped key per agent, read-only by default, write access added only when a lane needs it.

    Said by Nimrod, Nate Herk

    Video 1Video 2
  • Stay away
    Don't let an agent send, spend or delete without a human step

    Why: Sharbel A. sets Hermes to ask before spending, sending or deleting, and Jack Roberts says not to let it send email. Pav Rusovs keeps a locked-down settings file that blocks send, share and delete.

    Do this instead: Drafts only for email, approval gates for anything destructive, and a cap on how often a scheduled routine may run.

    Said by Sharbel A., Jack Roberts, Pav Rusovs

    Video 1Video 2Video 3Video 4
  • Stay away
    Don't put dashboards on the open internet

    Why: Julian Goldie lists a dashboard behind a VPN or SSH tunnel as the safe way to reach an agent remotely. Alex Finn, Nimrod and Pav Rusovs use Tailscale, a private network linking only your own devices.

    Do this instead: Reach the Gauntlet and the Hermes dashboards over Tailscale or a tunnel only.

    Said by Julian Goldie, Alex Finn, Nimrod, Pav Rusovs

    Video 1Video 2Video 3Video 4
  • Be careful
    Don't leave the server and its apps on defaults

    Why: Metics Media's baseline is a non-root sudo user, ed25519 SSH keys and a firewall allowing only SSH, 80 and 443. His Dokploy guide shows the Umami template shipping a default admin login of admin and umami, and he turns on weekly backups.

    Do this instead: Change defaults on day one, keep keys-only SSH, close every port Coolify does not need, and switch backups on.

    Said by Metics Media

    Video 1Video 2
  • Be careful
    Don't run agents without audits or monitoring

    Why: Tina Huang runs OpenClaw's security audit twice a day and her Hermes setup posts security reports to an alerts channel. NetworkChuck watches Hermes cron jobs, gateway and model logins with Checkmk. Wanderloots keeps the terminal in Docker so agent code stays boxed in.

    Do this instead: Schedule a recurring audit that reports to Sentinel's channel, never with secrets in the message.

    Said by Tina Huang, NetworkChuck, Wanderloots

    Video 1Video 2Video 3Video 4

Don't muddle memory

Context and architecture mistakes: what the agent reads every time, where facts live, and who may write where.

  • Stay away
    Don't let agents write into the human side of the vault

    Why: Eric Michaud splits his vault so agents may not edit the human side and the machine side is theirs. Wanderloots adds an allow-list so agents touch only approved vaults.

    Do this instead: Mark human-only and machine-writable folders in an agents file at the vault root, and archive rather than delete.

    Said by Eric Michaud, Wanderloots

    Video 1Video 2
  • Be careful
    Don't run two external memory providers at once

    Why: Sharbel A. says Hermes allows only one external provider at a time, among Honcho, Hindsight, Mem0 and Supermemory. Wanderloots gives his provider to the orchestrator alone. A catalogue note says Hindsight overlaps Chris's Qdrant plan.

    Do this instead: Choose one memory layer per agent, and decide between a provider and Qdrant before building either.

    Said by Sharbel A., Wanderloots

    Video 1Video 2Video 3
  • Be careful
    Don't let always-loaded files bloat

    Why: Soul, memory and instruction files are read every session. Jack Roberts's Context Doctor audits Hermes for bloat in the soul file, memory, skill descriptions, tools and config. Pav Rusovs keeps CLAUDE.md to about 40 lines as a map.

    Do this instead: Keep always-loaded files short, point to detail files, and send long reports to a documents area (Komputer Mechanic's Documents tab).

    Said by Jack Roberts, Pav Rusovs, Komputer Mechanic

    Video 1Video 2Video 3
  • Be careful
    Don't count on an instruction file as a hard rule

    Why: Mason Fitzgerald calls CLAUDE.md a soft instruction that is not enforced. Simon Scrapes describes hooks as deterministic checks that run when Claude says it is finished.

    Do this instead: Put must-never rules in permissions, hooks or scripts, and keep the instruction file for guidance.

    Said by Mason Fitzgerald, Simon Scrapes

    Video 1Video 2
  • Be careful
    Don't build a vector database on one presenter's benchmark

    Why: Mason Fitzgerald claims retrieval was 5.2 times faster and 3.5 times cheaper across 15 questions, and his package sits behind a paid community. Pav Rusovs measured a plain map at 30 seconds against 62 and 17k tokens against 28k.

    Do this instead: Run the same questions with and without Qdrant on Chris's own vault and compare time and tokens.

    Said by Mason Fitzgerald, Pav Rusovs

    Video 1Video 2
  • Be careful
    Don't run agents with no backup or way back

    Why: Jack Roberts recommends backing up the whole Hermes agent to GitHub daily. Wanderloots uses Git save points for the vault. Alex Finn suggests at least two profiles so one agent can repair the other.

    Do this instead: Back up each agent's config, soul and memory files daily, and keep a second agent able to fix the first.

    Said by Jack Roberts, Wanderloots, Alex Finn

    Video 1Video 2Video 3
  • Minor
    Don't build a wiki and never lint it

    Why: Tina Huang describes the LLM wiki as three jobs, ingest, query and lint, with an index and a log. Wanderloots uses scripts that check links and front matter, and Pav Rusovs runs a vault-lint skill.

    Do this instead: Schedule a weekly lint job that reports broken links and bad front matter.

    Said by Tina Huang, Wanderloots, Pav Rusovs

    Video 1Video 2Video 3

  • Hooks: how blocking works (Anthropic docs)From the web

    Hooks are set in settings files (user, project or local), in plugins, or in a skill's frontmatter. Events include PreToolUse, UserPromptSubmit, Stop and SessionStart. A hook that exits with code 2 blocks the action and sends its message back to Claude; other error codes let the action go ahead.

    1. Type /hooks to see every hook you have and where it comes from.

    For you: The right place for Chris's never-do rules, such as archive-not-delete.

    Watch out: Hooks run shell commands with your own permissions. A failing hook does not block by default.

    Claude Code docs: hooks reference web
  • Hooks (scripts that always run)

    Hooks are small scripts that fire on events, for example when Claude says it is finished or before it sees your prompt. Simon Scrapes calls them deterministic checks; Sharbel A. uses an output-filter hook that trims command output before the agent reads it.

    Claude Code hooks

    For you: Put must-never rules in hooks, not in CLAUDE.md, which Mason Fitzgerald calls a soft instruction.

    Paste This Into Claude Code, Never Run Out Of Tokens Again Sharbel A.Claude Changed Completely - Every NEW Concept Explained Simon ScrapesRAG Kills Notion, Obsidian, and Your "Second Brain" Mason Fitzgerald
  • Plugin marketplaces (Anthropic docs)From the web

    A marketplace is a catalogue of plugins. Anthropic's official one (claude-plugins-official) is added for you the first time you start Claude Code in a terminal. Others you add yourself; their plugins then appear in the /plugin panel's Discover tab.

    1. Type /plugin to browse.
    2. Add another marketplace with /plugin marketplace add owner/repo.
    3. Open a plugin's details and read what it will install before choosing a scope.

    For you: Sentinel reviews any non-official marketplace before it is added.

    Watch out: Plugins can run hooks and MCP servers. Auto-update is on for official marketplaces and off for community and third-party ones.

Then Claude sends exact actions like 'set this layer to 60% opacity' instead of looking at the screen and clicking, which is faster and has fewer misclicks.

  • What a Claude Code mod is

    A mod is a small add-on that changes how Claude Code looks and works: extra buttons, side panels, even a mini-game while Claude works. A skill tells Claude how to do a job and a connector plugs in another app; a mod changes Claude Code itself. It listens for events (such as Claude running a command) and can watch, change or handle them. Jay E says mods arrived on 1 October and work in the terminal and the desktop app's code tab.

    1. Update Claude Code to 2.1.287 or newer.
    2. Describe the mod you want; the built-in plugin-authoring skill builds it.
    3. Turn on hot reload to see it in this session.
    4. Ask Claude to save it as a plugin to keep it.
    Claude Code mods

    Watch out: Mods are temporary until saved as a plugin. Not in the VS Code extension when recorded. Any mod that calls a model uses your plan's usage.

    9 NEW Claude Mods Jay E, RoboNuggets

  • Output styles (built in)From the web

    An output style sets Claude's tone and response format for a whole session. Besides Default there are four built-ins: Proactive (starts work without routine questions), Concise (result first, no recap), Explanatory (adds short Insight blocks) and Learning (leaves small pieces of code for you).

    1. Type /output-style to list the styles.
    2. Type /output-style concise to switch.
    3. For your own style, save a Markdown file in ~/.claude/output-styles/.

    For you: Concise matches Chris's short-replies rule; a custom style could hold his neurodivergent-friendly format.

    Watch out: A style is an instruction, not a guarantee. Anything that must always happen belongs in a hook.

    Claude Code docs: output styles web
  • Status line (built in)From the web

    A custom bar at the bottom of Claude Code that runs your own script. Claude Code sends the script session data (model, context use, cost, git and more) and shows whatever it prints. It runs locally and uses no tokens.

    1. Type /statusline and describe what you want, for example: show model name and context percentage with a progress bar.
    2. Claude Code writes the script into ~/.claude/ and updates your settings.
    3. To remove it, type /statusline clear.

    For you: Colour-coded context and cost at a glance, which suits Chris's colour preference.

    Watch out: It runs a shell command, so it stays blank until you accept the folder's trust prompt.

    Claude Code docs: status line web

AAI operating system

What the videos mean by an "AI OS" or "Agent OS": one layer or dashboard where your agents, memory, tasks, schedules and tools run together. This tab shows each version the presenters built, the parts they share, how to build one, and what fits the Gauntlet.

From your videos: 44 of the 105 videos feed this tab. Only a few use the words "operating system" (Pav Rusovs, Jack Roberts, Julian Goldie, Max Mitcham, Tina Huang's HermesOS); the rest show the same idea as a mission control, dashboard, Kanban board or vault. Most finished AI OS builds shown are paid or unreleased, so the useful part is the pattern, not a product to install. Plus 14 entries from the web to fill gaps (marked From the web): Hermes's own dashboard, Kanban board and tutorial, Langfuse and OpenTelemetry tracing, Open WebUI as a front end, four open-source dashboards that exist today on GitHub, and four outside descriptions of an AI OS. The Paperclip entry now links its GitHub repo (its README lists Hermes as supported).

Hermes's own control room, per its docs (from the web) 6, A to Z

  • First Kanban board, per the Hermes tutorialFrom the web

    The tutorial's example uses two profiles, one doing work and one checking it, with the second task waiting on the first.

    1. Run hermes kanban init (optional; the first kanban command does it).
    2. Run hermes dashboard and click Kanban in the left menu.
    3. Create the first task with --assignee, and the second with --parent set to the first task's id.
    4. Start the dispatcher with hermes gateway start, or click Nudge dispatcher.
    5. Inspect results with hermes kanban show <id> and hermes kanban runs <id>.
    Hermes Kanban board

    For you: A test pair like Cerebra (research) then Brainiac (file to vault) would show the flow.

    Watch out: The tutorial does not explain how to create the profiles themselves.

    Hermes Kanban tutorial webHermes Kanban docs web
  • Hermes Kanban: the shared task boardFrom the web

    One board shared by all Hermes profiles, stored in ~/.hermes/kanban.db. Columns are triage, todo, ready, running, blocked, review, done and archived. A dispatcher inside the gateway checks every 60 seconds, moves todo to ready when parent tasks are done, and starts the assigned profile as its own process. Workers finish with complete, request review or block.

    Hermes Kanban boardHermes profiles

    For you: Matches the donts.json advice: try this native board before Paperclip or any meta layer.

    Watch out: Designed for one trusted host; avoid dependency loops, and note scratch workspaces are deleted on completion unless outputs are declared as artifacts. With hermes dashboard --host 0.0.0.0, every plugin route, the board included, is reachable from the network.

    Hermes Kanban docs web

    Checked 26 Oct 2026

  • hermes_otel: send traces to any monitoring toolFrom the web

    A community OpenTelemetry plugin (Apache-2.0) that exports each turn's model calls, tokens, cost, tool calls, sub-agents and approval waits. Tested with Phoenix, Langfuse, SigNoz, Jaeger, Grafana and others. With no backend set it keeps a local SQLite store and sends nothing.

    Watch out: Community tier, and content_capture defaults to full prompts and replies; set preview or off. Sentinel review first.

    hermes_otel plugin docs web
  • Hermes web dashboard: the built-in screenFrom the web

    hermes dashboard opens a local web app at 127.0.0.1:9119. Its pages: Status, Chat, Config, API Keys, Sessions, Logs, Analytics (tokens and cost over 7, 30 or 90 days), Cron, Profiles, Skills, MCP, Webhooks, Pairing, Channels and System.

    Hermes web dashboard

    For you: Analytics already shows cost per Hermes home; compare it with what the Gauntlet plans to show before building a duplicate.

    Watch out: Login is off on loopback and forced on for any other address; keep it on Tailscale or an SSH tunnel.

    Hermes web dashboard docs web

    Checked 26 Oct 2026

  • Langfuse plugin: traces and cost per turnFrom the web

    An official Hermes plugin sends one trace per turn to Langfuse, with each model call's tokens and cost, each tool call and sub-agent, and tags for platform, profile, cron job id and Kanban task. Langfuse itself is open source (MIT except its ee folders, about 36.5k stars) and can be self-hosted with Docker Compose.

    1. Install with hermes plugins install langfuse.
    2. Add HERMES_LANGFUSE_PUBLIC_KEY and HERMES_LANGFUSE_SECRET_KEY to the profile's .env (never in chat).
    3. For self-hosted Langfuse, also set HERMES_LANGFUSE_BASE_URL.
    4. Restart Hermes and check hermes plugins list shows it enabled.
    Langfuse

    For you: Per-profile and per-cron cost tags are what the Gauntlet's cost page needs; metadata mode suits Mantis.

    Watch out: Default mode is sanitized, which the docs call not a DLP guarantee; metadata mode sends no content. Telemetry can be lost if the queue fills.

    Hermes Langfuse plugin docs weblangfuse/langfuse on GitHub web
  • Open WebUI as a chat front end for HermesFrom the web

    Hermes has an OpenAI-compatible API server. Open WebUI connects to it like any OpenAI endpoint, Hermes runs its tools, and the answer streams back. The model appears as hermes-agent in Open WebUI's list.

    1. In ~/.hermes/.env set API_SERVER_ENABLED=true and an API_SERVER_KEY.
    2. Start the gateway with hermes gateway (default port 8642).
    3. In Open WebUI: Settings > Admin > Connections, add the URL ending in /v1 and the same key.
    Open WebUIHermes Agent

    For you: Chris already runs Open WebUI on Coolify, so this gives one chat screen for the agents.

    Watch out: In Docker on Linux, localhost and host.docker.internal may not reach Hermes; the docs list fixes.

    Open WebUI: connect Hermes Agent web

How others describe an AI operating system (from the web) 4, A to Z

  • AIOS (agiresearch): an agent OS kernelFrom the web

    An open-source research project that builds a kernel for agents: it schedules model calls and manages context, memory, storage and tools, with a separate Cerebrum SDK. Paper accepted to COLM 2025. About 6.5k stars; some deployment modes are still in development.

    Watch out: A research codebase, not a ready dashboard for a Hermes fleet.

    agiresearch/AIOS on GitHub web

    Checked 26 Oct 2026

  • Karpathy's LLM OSFrom the web

    In his talk "Intro to Large Language Models", Andrej Karpathy says LLMs can be thought of as the kernel process (the core program) of a new kind of operating system. The context window is like RAM, and the model pages information in and out of it, while using tools like a browser, files and other software.

    Karpathy LLM Wiki
    KDnuggets summary of the talk web
  • LLM as OS, agents as apps (research paper)From the web

    A 2023 paper by Ge and others maps an operating system onto AI: the LLM is the kernel, the context window is memory, outside storage is the file system, tools are devices and libraries, prompts are user commands, and agents are the apps.

    For you: In Chris's terms: OpenRouter models are the kernel, the vault is the file system, and the seven agents are the apps.

    arXiv 2312.03815 web
  • MemGPT: memory like an operating systemFrom the web

    The MemGPT paper (Packer and others, UC Berkeley) borrows virtual memory from operating systems: it moves information between fast and slow memory tiers so the model seems to have more context than it does, and uses interrupts to manage control flow.

    For you: The same tiering idea as Hermes memory plus the vault; useful background, not something to install.

    arXiv 2310.08560 web

How to build one 2, A to Z

  • Build an AI OS in eight steps

    This order is pieced together from the MAPS layers, the Hermes level videos and the mission-control builds. Each step works on its own before the next is added.

    1. Give each agent one lane, a soul file and a definition of done.
    2. Write a short map file that points to where memory lives.
    3. Pick one memory home (a markdown vault) and one external provider at most.
    4. Put routine work on cron jobs that return a decision; tick no-agent for script-only jobs.
    5. Use the native Kanban board for shared tasks and approvals.
    6. Have agents log what they did and save long reports to a documents area.
    7. Add a read-only dashboard over the logs, costs and schedules.
    8. Add monitoring and alerts so a stopped gateway reaches you.
    MAPS AI OS layersSOUL.mdHermes cron jobsHermes Kanban boardDocuments tab for long reportsCheckmk

  • Keep the OS safe

    The presenters add the same guard rails. Pav Rusovs blocks send, share and delete on the server so the agent can only draft email. Jack Roberts never pastes keys into chat and does not let Hermes send email. Nimrod gives agents scoped, read-only keys. Wanderloots caps turns in group rooms.

    1. Reach dashboards over Tailscale or a tunnel only.
    2. Block send, share and delete in a settings file.
    3. Keep keys in environment variables, never in chat.
    4. Give each agent its own scoped key.
    5. Cap turns and runs.

  • MAPS: Claude Code as an AI OS (Pav Rusovs)

    Four layers: Memory (a short CLAUDE.md map of about 40 lines plus signpost index files), Agent (Claude Code on laptop and VPS, synced every five minutes), Pulse (a routines.yaml list checked by a scheduler every five minutes, with a run cap) and Screen (a read-only live dashboard, "show, don't store"). He measured the map version at 30 seconds and 17k tokens against 62 seconds and 28k tokens without it.

    1. Write a short top-level map file that points to areas and holds no facts.

    3. Run the agent on an always-on server as well as the laptop.
    4. List routines, schedules and which machine runs each in one file.
    5. Add a run cap so a routine cannot loop.
    6. Build a read-only dashboard over the files.

What an AI OS is 3, A to Z

  • Agent anatomy: the parts every agent needs

    Tina Huang breaks a local agent into seven parts: a home (where it runs), a channel (how you talk to it), a brain (the model), memory, skills, a heartbeat (scheduled runs) and eyes (computer use). An AI OS is these parts made visible and shared across several agents. Her no-code agent video gives a similar list of six parts: model, tools, memory, audio, guardrails and orchestration.

    Agent anatomySix agent components
    Local AI Agents In 26 Minutes Tina HuangZero To Your First AI Agent In 26 Minutes (no code) channel unknown (presenter Tina; likely Tina Huang)
  • Agent harness versus AI OS

    Jack Roberts compares Hermes to a race team and Claude or ChatGPT to the drivers: Hermes is the system around the model. NetworkChuck calls Paperclip a "meta harness" that runs Hermes, Claude Code, Codex and Pi agents as one company. So an AI OS can sit on one harness (Hermes) or above several.

    Hermes AgentPaperclip
    Every Level of Hermes Agent Explained Jack Robertsyou need to try Paperclip RIGHT NOW! NetworkChuck
  • The idea in one line

    An AI OS is the layer that sits above your agents and ties them together. Jack Roberts describes his top Hermes level as "one operating system for every AI": memory, skills, documents, goals and spend in one place, so tools stop working in silos. Pav Rusovs calls it four layers on top of Claude Code. Tina Huang's version is a team of Hermes agents with shared boards and channels.

AAI road maps

Ordered paths from the videos: what to learn first, and what to build in what order, from chatbot to agents to automation. Each road map keeps the presenter's own order, and the last entry is a suggested order for Chris's own setup.

From your videos: 24 of the 105 videos feed this tab, and about 12 give a real ordered path (Tina Huang's skills roadmap, RPG class map, local AI by hardware and ways to run open models; the six- and seven-level Hermes guides; Sharbel A.'s Hermes curriculum; Dan Martell's AGENT framework). Learning paths lean on courses; few videos give a path for someone who already runs a fleet, so the last entry is assembled from several videos. Plus 9 entries from the web to fill gaps (marked From the web): Anthropic's agent guide, Anthropic Academy and its older GitHub courses, two DeepLearning.AI courses, the Hugging Face Agents and MCP courses, roadmap.sh's AI Agents and AI Engineer maps, and an ordered course path for a fleet owner.

Learning paths 8, in order

  • 1
    Essential AI skills: basic to advanced (Tina Huang)

    Three levels, each building on the last. Basics are for everyone, intermediate is about agents doing your own work, and advanced is for building for other people. She says the basics take days to weeks; real AI coding needs about two to three months of learning to code first.

    1. Basics: form a view on how much AI exposure your investments have.
    2. Basics: learn to prompt well; it underpins everything else.
    3. Basics: master a small core set of tools, starting with one general chatbot, then a research tool (Perplexity) and a learning tool (NotebookLM).
    4. Intermediate: use a web agent (her example is Manus) to learn how to hand over goals, not single requests.
    5. Intermediate: pick one local AI agent (Hermes or OpenClaw), choosing by how technical you are and open versus closed models.
    6. Advanced: build your own agents that are stable, reliable and low cost for others to use.
    7. Advanced: build MCP connections so agents can plug into apps and data.
    8. Advanced: AI coding (agentic engineering), only after you can code.
    Hermes AgentOpenClawPerplexityGemini NotebookManusModel Context Protocol

    For you: Chris is already at the intermediate level with Hermes; his CTO background makes the advanced steps realistic.

    Watch out: She warns that AI coding on top of weak coding skills does not get far.

    Updated Essential AI Skills For 2026 channel not stated (likely Tina Huang)
  • 2
    The RPG map: Tutorial Island, then pick a class (Tina Huang)

    Everyone starts on Tutorial Island with one starter course path, then picks one of six classes. She says you only need one course path, not several. Classes: Strategist (AI leadership), Rogue (hacking agents together), Alchemist (reliable agent systems for business), Crafter (AI-built apps), Sage (how models work, fine-tuning) and Machinist (AI on hardware).

    1. Learn what generative AI is and can do.
    2. Learn to prompt correctly.
    3. Learn the general tools: chat, deep research, image, video, audio, and bringing in your own data.
    4. Finish one starter path: Google AI Professional Certificate, deeplearning.ai, Elements of AI, Anthropic's free courses, or OpenAI's free courses.
    5. Choose a class using the prompt in her description.
    6. Follow that class's skill tree.
    AI learning coursesAnthropic courses

    Watch out: Vendor courses lean toward that vendor's own products; she notes the Anthropic and OpenAI courses both do this.

    Here's the AI Roadmap You Actually Need Tina Huang
  • 3
    Strategist class: leading AI in an organisation

    For people who set AI direction and lead adoption. Her first pick is OpenAI's free AI leadership course (about 3 to 4 hours), with Andrew Ng's AI for Everyone as an optional add-on that is older but has lasting team frameworks.

    1. Understand the vendor landscape and what each offers.
    2. Learn to run a mixed human and agent team: delegation norms and evaluation.
    3. Set strategy: where AI matters and the team's AI roadmap.
    4. Lead adoption: get buy-in and balance return on investment.
    5. Read Co-Intelligence and AI Snake Oil for the hopeful and sceptical views.
    AI learning coursesAI reading list

    For you: The class that matches Chris's CTO role.

    Here's the AI Roadmap You Actually Need Tina Huang
  • 4
    Rogue class: using agents and hacking them together

    For tinkerers who learn by doing. There is no general course; you pick one agent ecosystem (Claude, OpenAI, Microsoft Copilot, or open ones like Hermes and OpenClaw) and work through its docs. Along the way you learn gateways, memory, skills, security and self-hosting models.

    1. Learn what agents can do, how they differ from chatbots, and when they fail.
    2. Delegate real work to them and push the limits.
    3. Make the good workflows repeatable for daily use.
    4. Build your own agent setup that runs your life and work.
    Hermes AgentOpenClawClaude Cowork

    For you: Where Chris's seven-agent Hermes fleet already sits.

    Here's the AI Roadmap You Actually Need Tina Huang
  • 5
    Alchemist class: reliable agent systems

    For turning agents into dependable parts of business workflows. You choose a no-code route (Google Skills Agent Fundamentals or Vanderbilt's agentic AI course) or a code route (deeplearning.ai, Hugging Face agents course, Kaggle's AI agents intensive), then go deep on one platform. Everyone must learn reliability.

    1. Learn agent fundamentals.
    2. Build a first agent with tools and knowledge, then multi-agent setups.
    3. Learn evals and reliability (LangChain Academy, or Chip Huyen's AI Engineering book).
    4. Deploy, monitor, cost and integrate agents into existing workflows.

    Hermes in 31 minutes: the order to learn it (Sharbel A.)

    A beginner mental model for Hermes, taught in this order. His core rule: memory holds facts, skills hold repeatable procedures, and cron jobs should be self-contained and return a decision.

    1. Surfaces: desktop app as the control room, Telegram on the phone.

    8. Sub-agents: narrow parallel workers checked by the main agent.
    9. Profiles: separate agents with their own keys, memory, cron and persona.

Build paths 9, in order

  • 1
    Six levels of Hermes (Metics Media)

    A ladder you climb without skipping steps, each with a small "level up" task. He hands over trust in a set order: let the agent read and organise for a few weeks, then draft, and sending on its own comes last if ever. When anything misbehaves, check credit, gateway and logs.

    1. Give it a home: an always-on server and a model provider.
    2. Reach it from anywhere: Telegram by QR code, the desktop app and voice.
    3. Put it to work in your own files and accounts, using a separate account for the agent and sharing only chosen folders.
    4. Train it: correct it once, update its soul, and use /learn to turn a document into a skill.
    5. Hand it a weekly chore: create the job paused, read what it wrote, then switch it on.
    6. Give it a team with a Kanban project board.

    Seven levels of Hermes (Jack Roberts)

    From one-shot prompts to an agentic operating system. He estimates savings rise from about 30 minutes a day at level one to about a day a week at level three. Each level adds one habit.

    1. Beginner: install Hermes, connect a chat app, use it for simple tasks, and collaborate rather than one-shot.
    2. Apprentice: let memory build and give it a soul.md about you.
    3. Commands and models: use /steer, /background and /model; pick the right model per task; add skills with a model chosen per skill.
    4. Integrator: connect email, calendar, Notion, Slack and meeting notes, often through MCP; keep the list short.
    5. Orchestration: a lead agent runs sub-agents on different models in parallel.
    6. Builder: build software remotely and add scheduled tasks so work happens without you.
    7. Agentic power user: one operating system joining memory, skills, documents and spend across every AI tool.

    Ways to run open-source models (Tina Huang)

    Four main categories plus two advanced bonus ones, presented in this order. She calls the browser playground the easiest of all, and fine-tuning locally one of the hardest jobs.

    1. Local: download a model manager such as Ollama and chat offline; fine-tuning locally needs a GPU and Unsloth.

    3. API providers: Groq, Together AI or Fireworks AI host the model and you call an API key.

    5. Bonus, managed cloud: scales for you; for startups that need scale.
    6. Bonus, on-device: the model ships inside an app on the user's device.

    Local AI by hardware size (Tina Huang)

    From microcontrollers to rented data-centre GPUs. Her sizing rule: take 75 percent of RAM as usable, divide by 0.6, and that is roughly the largest model in billions of parameters.

    1. Microcontroller (Arduino Uno R4, ESP32-S3): tiny story models.

    6. AMD Ryzen AI Halo (128 GB): Llama 3.3 70B and GPT-OSS 120B.
    7. Rented 8x H100: the largest models and video generation.

    A suggestion, not a plan he has agreed to. Design 4, in order

  • 1
    Mock up the page in Claude Design

    Jason Lee typed /design and asked for a landing page that shows every feature, told Claude to treat it as its design resume, and gave it a reference site. Claude added scrolling and animated sections he had not asked for, built with code rather than video. He used the Higgsfield MCP to make the images.

    1. Type /design and describe the page in two or three lines.
    2. Paste a link to a site whose style you like.
    3. Ask it to use the Higgsfield MCP for any images.
    4. Compare the result with the reference so it borrows ideas, not the copy.
    Claude DesignHiggsfield

    For you: Chris asked for design mock-ups in Claude Design before anything is built, so this is step one for any of his sites.

    I Had Claude Opus 5.5 Build a Mobile App, Website and Motion Graphics Video (Shocking Results!) Jason Lee7 Free GitHub Repos That Make Claude So Good It Feels Illegal AI Edge
  • 2
    Add one website design skill

    Julian Goldie installed UI UX Pro Max into Codex by pasting its GitHub link and saying 'install this skill for website design'. He says you can either give a design skill or a screenshot of what you want; without either, pages look bland. Jack Roberts made his own skill, Power Design, with about 20 design rules such as the golden ratio.

    1. Pick one design skill and have Sentinel review it.
    2. Paste its link and ask the agent to install it.
    3. Give it facts about you and the site in the same prompt.

Build 3, in order

  • 1
    Preview on your own computer first

    Both Jason Lee and Julian Goldie run the site on localhost, meaning only on your own machine, and click through it in Chrome before anything goes online. Julian notes Codex also has its own preview pane. You get the first 80% fast; the rest is feedback.

    1. Ask: 'Serve this on localhost so I can test every button.'
    2. Open the link in your browser.
    3. Tell the agent exactly what you dislike or what broke.
    4. Repeat until it feels right.
    CodexClaude Code
    I Had Claude Opus 5.5 Build a Mobile App, Website and Motion Graphics Video (Shocking Results!) Jason LeeGPT 6 Astra AI Full COURSE 1 HOUR (Build & Automate Anything) Julian Goldie SEO
  • 2
    Let an agent build and ship a small site

    Alex Finn had Grok Bot build a micro-business site. Its built-in Cursor cloud agents made the first live version in about two minutes. He then connected Vercel for hosting, GitHub for the code, Resend for email, Stripe for payments and Google Search Console for search, and the bot asks his approval before outside actions.

    1. Pick a simple site idea; the name does not need to be perfect.
    2. Connect GitHub so code and changes are stored.
    3. Connect a host such as Vercel.
    4. Add email, payments and search tools only when needed.

  • 6
    Turn on Row Level Security for every tableFrom the web

    Supabase says to enable Row Level Security (RLS, rules for who sees which rows) on every table the API can reach. Without it, the table is open. Once on, no data comes through the public key until you add policies.

    1. For each table, run: alter table public.<table> enable row level security;
    2. Add a policy so each user sees only their own rows.
    3. Test with two accounts.
    Supabase

    Watch out: The 2025 Lovable data leak came from weak RLS rules (see the 'Vibe coding' tab).

    Checked 26 Oct 2026

  • 7
    Publishable key in the app, secret key on the serverFrom the web

    Supabase's publishable key is safe in web pages and apps because RLS limits it. The secret key bypasses RLS and gives full access, so it belongs only in server code, never in the browser, a shipped app or git. The old JWT-based anon and service_role keys are legacy; Supabase recommends moving to the new keys (the end-of-2026 phase-out date could not be confirmed on the current page).

    1. If a secret key leaks, fix the cause first.
    2. Create a new key under Settings > API Keys.
    3. Replace it everywhere, then delete the old one.
    SupabaseDoppler

    Back up Coolify databases, and test a restoreFrom the web

    Coolify can back up PostgreSQL, MySQL, MariaDB, MongoDB, ClickHouse and SQLite on a schedule, to the server and to S3 storage (offsite cloud storage). Coolify's docs stress that a backup only proves a file exists; restore one into a spare database to prove it works.

    1. Open the database, then Backups > + Add.
    2. Pick a schedule, such as daily.
    3. Turn on S3 storage for an offsite copy.
    4. Click Back up now and check it shows success with a size above zero.
    5. Restore a copy into a test database.

    Watch out: Redis, Dragonfly and KeyDB are not covered; they need their own backups.

  • 7
    Back up Coolify itself, plus its APP_KEYFrom the web

    A Coolify instance backup saves projects and settings, not app data. Coolify's APP_KEY encrypts saved secrets, and it is not in the backup (S3 instance backups hold only the database file). Without it, restored secrets cannot be read.

    1. Go to Settings > Backup and click Back up now.
    2. Download a copy and keep it off the server.
    3. Store the APP_KEY from /data/coolify/source/.env somewhere safe.

    Watch out: The APP_KEY is a secret: never post it in Discord.

    Coolify docs: Back up Coolify web

  • Connect Claude Code or Codex to XcodeFrom the web

    If you run Claude Code or Codex in Terminal, Xcode can lend it its tools, such as building your app. This works through MCP (a standard plug for AI tools), using Xcode's own bridge. Xcode shows an alert when an outside agent connects.

  • iPad apps must now resize like windowsFrom the web

    Since iPadOS 26, the old setting that kept an app full screen (UIRequiresFullScreen) is deprecated. From iOS 27 and iPadOS 27, for apps built with the iOS 27 SDK, it no longer stops resizing, and a launch screen is required for App Store submission. Apple asks apps to support all orientations and adapt when the window changes size.

    1. Check the app has a launch screen.
    2. Support all orientations.
    3. Remove UIRequiresFullScreen from Info.plist.
    4. Ask the agent to test layouts at several window sizes.

    For you: Give Cyborg this note as a rule for any iPad build.

    Watch out: Apple warns that apps that do not update may show broken or misplaced layouts.

  • Ship a Mac app outside the Mac App StoreFrom the web

    A Mac app you give out yourself must be signed with a Developer ID certificate and notarized, meaning Apple scans it and stamps it. Gatekeeper, the Mac's install guard, checks for this. Xcode's Distribute App has a 'Direct Distribution' option that notarizes for you.

    1. Turn on the hardened runtime capability in Xcode.
    2. Choose Product > Archive.
    3. In the Organizer, click Distribute App, then Direct Distribution.
    4. Test the downloaded app on a Mac before sharing.

    Watch out: Only the Account Holder can create a Developer ID certificate. For a Mac Catalyst app, make separate iPad and Mac archives.

    Apple: Signing your apps for Gatekeeper webApple: Distributing your app for beta testing and releases web

Wiring the stack 6, A to Z

  • Coolify server on the private networkFrom the web

    Goal: Reach Coolify and admin ports only over Tailscale. Coolify offers a Tailscale Client service so a deployment can join your tailnet. Coolify's docs say that if you lock down port 22, allow SSH from the Tailscale range (100.x.x.x/10), because Coolify needs SSH to deploy. Tailscale's Personal plan is free for up to 6 users with unlimited devices.

    TailscaleHostinger VPS

    For you: Extends 'Reach every device privately' to the VPS itself; Sentinel reviews firewall changes before they go in.

    Watch out: Changing SSH rules can lock you out; keep a console login from the host's panel ready.

    Coolify docs: Tailscale Client service webTailscale pricing web
  • Home Assistant as a tool for agentsFrom the web

    Goal: Let an AI client check and control the house. Home Assistant (since 2025.2) has a Model Context Protocol Server integration. You copy the server URL from Settings > System > AI into the client and sign in with OAuth. Clients can only touch the devices you expose.

    Home Assistant

    For you: Alfred could answer 'is the garage door shut?' in his channel, with only a few devices exposed.

    Watch out: Cloud-hosted agents need Home Assistant reachable from the internet, for example through Home Assistant Cloud; that widens exposure.

    Home Assistant: Model Context Protocol Server web
  • Move repeat agent jobs into workflows

    Goal: lower AI cost and more dependable jobs. After hitting 96% of his weekly Grok allowance, one host had his Zapier agent go through his team's work and find jobs that could become zaps. Zaps wait for webhooks (a ping when something happens) and run code, so they are cheaper and steadier than an agent checking constantly. Anything needing judgment is handed back to the agent.

    1. List jobs your agents run on a timer.
    2. Mark the ones with no real judgment.
    3. Rebuild those as workflows triggered by webhooks.
    4. Keep the agent only for the judgment step.
    n8nZapier MCP

    For you: Chris already runs n8n, so the same move works there with no new subscription.

    Watch out: The episode was Zapier-sponsored; Zapier says it has a free-forever plan.

    Copy viral videos, change your TV's OS... The Next New Thing
  • n8n workflows as agent tools (MCP)From the web

    Goal: Let an agent call your n8n workflows like tools. The MCP Server Trigger turns an n8n workflow into an MCP server; clients connect by URL over SSE or streamable HTTP. Each workflow you expose becomes one tool.

    1. Add an MCP Server Trigger to a new workflow.
    2. Attach a Custom n8n Workflow Tool for each workflow to expose.
    3. Set Bearer or Header auth.
    4. Publish, then give the production URL to the MCP client.
    n8n

    For you: Cerebra or Alfred could trigger vetted n8n flows without being given n8n admin rights.

    Watch out: n8n docs: behind a reverse proxy, turn off buffering and gzip for the MCP path or connections break.

    n8n docs: MCP Server Trigger web
  • Obsidian vault over MCPFrom the web

    Goal: Let an MCP client read, search and append to the vault. The Local REST API plugin opens an HTTPS API on 127.0.0.1:27124 with a bearer key, and now has a built-in MCP server. The separate mcp-obsidian server uses that plugin and offers tools such as search, get file, append and patch.

    1. Install the Local REST API community plugin and copy its API key.
    2. Connect an MCP client, either to the plugin's built-in server or through mcp-obsidian.
    3. Set OBSIDIAN_API_KEY (and host and port if not the defaults).
    Obsidian

    For you: Works only while Obsidian is open on that Mac; the agents on the VPS already use the GitHub copy of the vault instead.

    Watch out: mcp-obsidian includes a delete_file tool; Chris's rule is archive, never delete, and the archive folder is off limits, so Sentinel should scope it first.

    Obsidian Local REST API plugin (GitHub) webmcp-obsidian (GitHub) web
  • OpenRouter models inside n8nFrom the web

    Goal: Use the same OpenRouter account in n8n as the agents do. n8n's OpenRouter Chat Model node plugs into its AI Agent nodes and lists only models your key can use. It has options for temperature, JSON output, timeouts and retries.

    1. Add OpenRouter credentials in n8n.
    2. Add an AI Agent node and attach the OpenRouter Chat Model.
    3. Pick the model and a low temperature for factual jobs.
    4. Set a timeout and max retries.
    n8nOpenRouter

    For you: Give n8n its own OpenRouter key with a spend limit, so its costs show apart from the agents'.

    n8n docs: OpenRouter Chat Model node webOpenRouter pricing web

Agents 14, A to Z

    An agent is an AI model that has been given tools, memory and a job. It can take steps on its own, not just answer one question. Tina Huang lists six parts: model, tools, memory, audio, guardrails and orchestration. Everyday picture: a new staff member with a desk, a phone and a to-do list, instead of a phone line you call with one question.

Connecting tools 14, A to Z

  • A2A protocol (Agent2Agent)From the web

    A2A is an open standard for agents from different makers to find each other and share work. Each agent publishes an 'agent card', a small JSON file listing what it does and how to reach it. Google started it in April 2025 and donated it to the Linux Foundation, which now runs it as an open-source project. It complements MCP: MCP connects an agent to tools, A2A connects agents to agents. Everyday picture: business cards plus a shared work-order format between firms.

    Agent Communication Protocol

    For you: Chris's agents talk through Discord inside one Hermes setup, so A2A is not needed today; it matters if he mixes agent products.

    Watch out: IBM described it as early-stage in mid-2025; check what Hermes supports before planning on it.

  • Fallback providers

  • Fine-tuning vs promptingFrom the web

    Prompting means giving a model better instructions and examples each time. Fine-tuning means training a copy of the model on many examples so the behaviour is built in. OpenAI says prompting may be all you need, and fine-tuning helps mainly with large example sets, shorter prompts and cheaper small models. Everyday picture: a clear checklist for a temp worker vs sending them on a training course.

    For you: Chris's agents run on prompts, soul files and skills; nothing in the setup needs fine-tuning.

    Watch out: As of Oct 2026 OpenAI's page says its fine-tuning platform is winding down and closed to new users; existing users can still run training jobs for the coming months.

    OpenAI docs: Model optimization (fine-tuning) web

    Checked 26 Oct 2026

  • HallucinationFrom the web

    A hallucination is when a model states something false or not supported by the material it was given, often in a confident tone. Anthropic's advice: allow the model to say 'I don't know', ask for direct quotes and citations, and limit it to the documents you supply. These steps reduce it but do not remove it. Everyday picture: a keen witness who fills gaps in memory with guesses.

    For you: Cerebra's research and any family-history findings should carry a source link for each claim.

    Watch out: Anthropic says to always check important facts yourself, especially for high-stakes decisions.

    Claude docs: Reduce hallucinations web

    Checked 26 Oct 2026

  • Knowledge cutoffFrom the web

    A model only knows the world up to the date its training data stops. Anthropic lists a 'reliable knowledge cutoff' for each model; for Claude Haiku 5.5 it is June 2026. Anything newer must come from a tool such as web search or your own files. Everyday picture: a well-read friend who has been at sea since June.

    Claude Haiku

    For you: Cerebra's web search is how the fleet learns about anything after a model's cutoff.

  • Local vs cloud models

    A cloud model runs on a company's servers and you pay per use. A local model runs on your own computer: private and free per use, but limited by your memory and chip. Tina Huang's rule: take 75 percent of your RAM and divide by 0.6 to get the billions of parameters that fit. Everyday picture: eating out versus cooking at home: home is cheaper per meal, but you buy the kitchen first.

    OllamaLM StudioLocal models settingRAM-to-model-size rule

    For you: Chris's agents use cloud models today; a local model could take simple jobs if a Mac is sized for it.

    Watch out: Local quality is lower, and hardware costs up front (Alex Finn prices a DGX Spark at about 4,800 USD).

  • QuantizationFrom the web

In GGUF files used by Ollama and LM Studio, a name like Q4_K means about 4 bits per weight. Everyday picture: saving a photo as a smaller JPEG; it fits on the phone, with slight blur.

CConnecting Hermes to control your phone

How the videos say to reach a Hermes agent from your phone, talk to it by voice, and in the newest release let it tap your phone's screen. Chris uses an iPhone, so each part flags what works on iPhone and what is Android only.

From your videos: About 20 of the 105 videos touch phone use. Only one, 'Hermes Agent Can Now CONTROL Your Phone!', covers true phone control, and its captions were Arabic so one name is low-confidence. Plus 12 entries from the web to fill gaps (marked From the web): Hermes's own platform docs, iMessage via BlueBubbles, ntfy and Pushover alerts, Shortcuts and Siri, Apple's iPhone Mirroring rules, ADB and mobile-mcp, and Tailscale on phones.

Apple Shortcuts and Siri (iPhone only) 2, A to Z

  • Apple Shortcuts can call a web addressFrom the web

    Apple's Shortcuts app on iPhone and iPad has a 'Get Contents of URL' action that makes a web request and can send JSON, a form or a file. That is how a Shortcut can hand a message to an agent's webhook or notification topic.

    Apple Shortcuts

    For you: iPhone and iPad only. Pairs with ntfy or an n8n webhook.

    Apple: Request your first API in Shortcuts web

    Checked 26 Oct 2026

  • 'Hey Siri' to reach your agentFrom the web

    Siri runs any shortcut when you say its name, on iPhone, iPad, HomePod, Apple Watch or Mac. Combine that with the ntfy channel: a shortcut that posts your words to the agent's ntfy topic, and the reply comes back as a push.

    1. Set up Hermes's ntfy channel with a private topic.
    2. Make a shortcut that asks for text, then uses Get Contents of URL to POST it to the topic.
    3. Give the shortcut a short name, such as 'Ask Alfred'.
    4. Say 'Hey Siri, Ask Alfred'.

  • ntfy: a lightweight push channel to talk to HermesFrom the web

    ntfy is a simple push-notification service. Hermes supports it as a channel: subscribe to a topic in the ntfy phone app, send a message to that topic, and the agent's reply arrives as a push notification. It works with the free ntfy.sh server or a self-hosted one.

    For you: Works on iPhone and Android. Self-hosting on Coolify would keep it private.

    Watch out: The Hermes docs say anyone who knows the topic name can talk to the agent. Use a self-hosted topic with access control, a reserved topic with a token, or at least a long unguessable name, and send nothing sensitive otherwise. ntfy caps each message at 4,096 characters; Hermes cuts longer replies.

  • Check whether a skill actually helps

  • Find what is eating your Claude Code limits

    Sharbel A. shows four built-in views and a check on connected tools.

    1. Run /context and read what fills the window line by line.
    2. Check the tools line says 'deferred' (manuals load only when needed).
    3. Open the MCP panel and switch off servers you have not used in a month.
    4. Run /usage to see which skill, tool or agent used the most.
    5. Look at any scheduled tasks: if they run less than once an hour, each run misses the cache.

  • Keep a Claude Code session lean

    Sharbel A. says almost all usage is the agent re-reading history, not what you type. These habits cut it.

    1. Use /clear when you switch to a different job (first /rename the session so /resume can bring it back).
    2. Pick model and effort at the start and leave them; changing them mid-session reprocesses the whole chat.
    3. Use /rewind instead of compacting if you only need to undo a few turns.
    4. Paste text instead of screenshots, and turn PDFs into plain text first.
    5. Set sub-agents to Haiku for grunt work.
    /clear (Claude Code)Claude Code

    For you: Forge and Cyborg/Vic do the coding work; Chris's agents already run on Haiku.

    Watch out: He says compacting is the most expensive message of a session and wipes the cache.

Discord: one bot per agent 4, A to Z

  • Copy Discord IDs with Developer ModeFrom the web

    Hermes's channel and user settings need Discord IDs, not names. Developer Mode adds a Copy ID option to right-click menus.

    1. Desktop: User Settings (cog, bottom left) > Advanced > turn on Developer Mode.
    2. Phone: tap your avatar, then the cog, scroll to Advanced under App Settings, and turn on Developer Mode.
    3. Channel ID: right-click the channel (long-press on phone) > Copy Channel ID.
    4. Your user ID: right-click your name > Copy User ID.
    5. Server ID: right-click the server icon > Copy Server ID.
    Discord

    For you: Needed for DISCORD_ALLOWED_USERS and DISCORD_ALLOWED_CHANNELS in each agent's settings.

    Discord support: Find your user, server or message ID web
  • Keep each agent in its own Discord channelFrom the web

    Hermes has settings that limit where a bot answers. Set an allowed channel list, and the bot replies only there; DMs are handled separately.

    1. Copy the channel ID for the agent's channel (see Developer Mode).
    2. In the agent's ~/.hermes/.env set DISCORD_ALLOWED_CHANNELS to that ID (comma-separate several).
    3. Set DISCORD_ALLOWED_USERS to your own user ID so only you can use it.
    4. Optional: DISCORD_FREE_RESPONSE_CHANNELS for channels where it answers without an @mention (otherwise it needs a mention).
    5. Optional: DISCORD_IGNORED_CHANNELS for channels it must never answer in, even when mentioned.
    6. Restart the gateway and test in an allowed and a not-allowed channel.
    Discordhermes gateway restart

    For you: Matches Chris's channel-per-agent layout; Mantis's private channel is a good first candidate for a tight allowlist.

    Watch out: Leave DISCORD_ALLOW_MENTION_EVERYONE and DISCORD_ALLOW_MENTION_ROLES off (false is the default), or a model reply with @everyone pings the whole server.

    Hermes Agent docs: Discord web

    Checked 26 Oct 2026

  • Make a Discord bot for one agentFrom the web

    Hermes's Discord page gives the full path: a Discord app, a bot user, two switches turned on, a token, and an invite link. Repeat it once per agent so each has its own name and token.

    1. In the Discord Developer Portal, click New Application, name it after the agent and click Create. Note the Application ID.
    2. Open Bot. Under Privileged Gateway Intents, turn on Message Content Intent and Server Members Intent, then Save Changes.
    3. Under Token, click Reset Token and copy it straight into the agent's .env as DISCORD_BOT_TOKEN. It is shown only once.
    4. Run hermes gateway setup and pick Discord. It checks the token, warns if Message Content is off, and prints an invite link.
    5. Open the invite link (scopes bot and applications.commands) and add the bot to your server. You need Manage Server.
    6. Let the wizard allowlist you as owner, then start it with hermes gateway and send it a test message.
    Discord

    For you: One bot per agent (Alfred, Brainiac, Cerebra and so on) keeps each agent's channel and token separate.

    Watch out: Without Message Content Intent Discord refuses the connection and the bot stays offline. Never post the token in Discord.

    Hermes Agent docs: Discord web

    Checked 26 Oct 2026

    A private channel is hidden from everyone except the roles or members you add. You need admin rights on the server.

Hermes: running bigger work 6, A to Z

  • Cut model costs with routing

    Use a strong model for hard work and a cheap one for background jobs. Python Simplified sets a free model for 'auxiliary' tasks; Sharbel A. says you can just tell Hermes which model to use for what.

    1. Add a second provider: in the Hermes terminal type hermes model and follow the prompts.
    2. Pick a cheap or free model for it.
    3. In the Models menu, set your main model for reasoning and chat.
    4. Next to the cheap model, use the 'use as' selector and give it the auxiliary tasks.
    5. Or tell Hermes in plain words: use model A for coding and tool work, model B for cron jobs.
    6. Check spend on your provider's activity page after a few days.
    Main and auxiliary model splitOpenRouterhermes setup and hermes model

    For you: Chris runs Claude Haiku via OpenRouter; confirm any model name on OpenRouter's own list before switching an agent.

    Watch out: Sharbel A.: a weak model on hard multi-step work can cost more in retries than a strong one.

  • Run a long job with /goal

    /goal keeps Hermes working until the goal is met. Sharbel A. first asks Hermes to design the goal prompt, then answers its questions.

    1. Send: 'I want to run a /goal with you, but first help me design the perfect /goal prompt. Ask me any clarifying questions.'
    2. Ask it to include success criteria, constraints, files to inspect, tools, deliverables, safety rules and how to verify.
    3. Answer its questions (he used one voice note).
    4. Copy the prompt it writes and run it as /goal.
    5. Come back later and check the result against the success criteria.
    Hermes /goal

    For you: Good for Cyborg/Vic's code work; keep goals read-only until checked.

    Watch out: Jack Roberts says /goal runs with a turn budget; keep a cap so it cannot loop forever.

Hermes: safety and fixing 5, A to Z

  • Fix a bot that stopped replying

    Metics Media's troubleshooting order: read the logs, restart the gateway, then restart the whole app.

    1. Open Logs in the web dashboard and filter for errors and warnings.
    2. Click Restart Gateway, confirm, and wait for status 'running'.

    NetworkChuck monitors his Hermes agent with Checkmk and sends an alert to Slack when its gateway goes down, then a recovery message.

    1. In Checkmk, go to Setup, then Notifications, and click Add notification rule.
    2. Keep the default filters, or limit them to the agent's host and its gateway service.
    3. Choose Slack as the method and add the webhook.
    4. Set the recipient (he uses cmkadmin) and apply.
    5. Test by stopping the gateway and waiting about a minute for the alert.

  • Make a Hermes cron job that returns a decision

    A cron job is a task Hermes runs on a timer. Sharbel A. says each run starts in a fresh session, so the prompt must stand on its own. A good job says what to check, where, what counts, what to ignore and where to send the result.

    1. Pick one thing you want watched and the decision you want back.
    2. Write the prompt with: what to check, where, what is important, what to ignore, and where to deliver.
    3. Example from the video: every morning at 8:00, check the last 24 hours and return one urgent issue, one opportunity and one recommended action, under 12 bullet points.
    4. Send the prompt to Hermes in chat, or ask it to create the cron for you.
    5. Open the Cron (Scheduled Jobs) page and check the time, the frequency and the exact prompt it saved.
    6. Use pause or run-by-hand on that page to test it once.
    Hermes cron jobsMorning brief cronHermes web dashboard

    For you: Alfred owns briefings; deliver each job to that agent's own Discord channel, not a shared one.

    Watch out: Sharbel A. lists 'making every idea a cron job' as a top mistake: a job with no clear decision becomes notification spam.

  • Run a script-only cron job without paying a model

    1. In the Hermes Files menu, create a folder named exactly 'scripts' and upload your script there.

n8n: schedules and webhooks 4, A to Z

  • Get told when an n8n workflow failsFrom the web

    n8n can run a second 'error workflow' whenever a workflow fails. One error workflow can watch many workflows.

    1. Make a new workflow that starts with the Error Trigger node.
    2. Add what should happen, for example a Discord node posting to an alerts channel.
    3. Name it (for example Error Handler) and save it.
    4. In each workflow to watch, open Options > Settings, pick it under Error workflow, and save.
    n8nDiscord

    For you: Pairs with the Hermes gateway alert how-to so both n8n and agents report failures to one place.

    n8n docs: Error handling web

    Checked 26 Oct 2026

  • Post n8n results into a Discord channel with a webhookFrom the web

    For one-way messages (reports, alerts) a Discord webhook is enough: no bot user, no login. It can only post, not listen.

    1. In Discord: Server Settings > Integrations > Create Webhook.
    2. Name it, and choose the channel in the CHANNEL dropdown.
    3. Click Copy Webhook URL.
    4. In n8n, make a Discord credential of type Webhook and paste the URL.
    5. Add a Discord node to the workflow using that credential, and run a test.
    n8nDiscord

    For you: Fits an n8n alert channel; agents that must reply still need their own bot.

    Watch out: Anyone with the webhook URL can post into that channel, so treat it like a secret.

    n8n docs: Discord credentials web
  • Run an n8n workflow on a scheduleFrom the web

    The Schedule Trigger starts a workflow every so many minutes, hours or days, or on a cron pattern (a 5-part time rule). It runs only when the workflow is saved and published.

    1. Add a Schedule Trigger as the first node.
    2. Pick a unit (Seconds, Minutes, Hours, Days, Weeks, Months) or Custom (Cron). Example: 0 9 * * 1-5 is 09:00 on weekdays.
    3. Set the workflow's time zone in its settings, or it uses the server's (self-hosted default is America/New_York).
    4. In Settings, choose what happens to runs missed during downtime (default: skip them).
    5. Save and publish the workflow.
    n8n

    For you: Whitby is in the same time zone as New York, but set America/Toronto explicitly so it is clear.

    Watch out: If a cron rule uses a variable, changing it later does nothing until you unpublish and republish.

    n8n docs: Schedule Trigger node web

    Checked 26 Oct 2026

  • Start an n8n workflow from a webhookFrom the web

    A Webhook node gives the workflow its own web address. A test address works while you listen in the editor; the real one works only after you publish.

    1. Add a Webhook node as the trigger.
    2. Choose the method (for example POST) and, if you like, a path.
    3. Choose authentication: Basic, Header, JWT or n8n User Auth. Do not leave it on None for anything real.
    4. Choose when it replies: at once, when the last node finishes, or via a Respond to Webhook node.
    5. Copy the test URL, click Listen for Test Event, and send a test request.
    6. Publish the workflow to switch on the production URL; its runs show under Executions.
    n8n

    For you: A way for a Hermes agent or a phone shortcut to kick off an n8n job; pair it with a schedule for a daily run plus on-demand runs.

    Watch out: Payloads over 16 MB are refused unless N8N_PAYLOAD_SIZE_MAX is raised.

    n8n docs: Webhook node web

    Checked 26 Oct 2026

Tailscale 2, A to Z

  • Share a private page with Tailscale ServeFrom the web

    Tailscale Serve puts a local web page on an HTTPS address that only your own Tailscale devices can open. Funnel is the public version; do not use it for dashboards.

    1. Start the page on the machine, for example on port 3000.
    2. Run: tailscale serve 3000
    3. If HTTPS is not yet on for your tailnet, the command walks you through turning it on.
    4. Open the address it prints (device-name.tailnet-name.ts.net) from another Tailscale device.
    5. Press Ctrl+C to stop sharing.
    Tailscale ServeTailscale

    For you: Fits Chris's rule that dashboards are reached over Tailscale or a tunnel only (see the 'Don't put dashboards on the open internet' warning).

    Watch out: One port is either Serve (private) or Funnel (public): the last command wins. Funnel is enabled on devices by default, so turn it off if unused.

    Tailscale docs: Tailscale Serve web

    Checked 26 Oct 2026

  • Stop the server dropping off TailscaleFrom the web

    Device keys expire after 180 days by default (for new tailnets), and an expired server disappears from the tailnet. Tailscale suggests turning expiry off for trusted servers.

    1. Open the Machines page of the admin console.
    2. Find the server's row.
    3. Open the … menu on the right and choose Disable Key Expiry.
    4. Leave expiry on for the Mac, iPhone and iPad.
    Tailscale

    Watch out: If a key does expire, do not run tailscale up --force-reauth over a Tailscale-only SSH session; you can cut yourself off. Keep the Hostinger browser terminal as a way in.

    Tailscale docs: Key expiry web

    Checked 26 Oct 2026

  • Cerebra reads a company's filings on SEDAR+ (Canada) or EDGAR (US)From the web

    Goal: understand a company from its own documents, not from social media. SEDAR+ is the CSA's free filing system for Canadian public companies: annual reports, interim financial statements and press releases. Safety and scams 6, A to Z

  • 'Agentic income' claims are small

    Alex Finn says his agent-run site has made $1,100, all from two sponsorships, and talks of several such businesses one day replacing a job. Dubibubi's agent-run Etsy shop made $4.55 in 10 days.

  • 'AI washing': firms that lie about using AI (US case)From the web

    In October 2024 the US SEC settled charges against Rimar Capital, which raised nearly $4 million (USD) from 45 investors while falsely saying it used an AI platform to trade. Shown here as a US example of the pattern Canadian regulators also warn about.

    Watch out: 'Uses AI' in a pitch proves nothing; ask for registration, not technology claims.

  • Check a 'hot tip' or 'AI trading bot' claim before you actFrom the web

    Goal: catch a scam in two minutes. The OSC warns that scammers sell 'AI trading bots' that may not use AI at all, let you withdraw small amounts first to build trust, use deepfake celebrity videos, and push urgency. Its first tip: check whether the person or firm is registered.

    1. Paste the pitch to the agent and ask which OSC warning signs it shows.
    2. Look up the firm on the CSA National Registrant Search or CIRO AdvisorReport yourself.
    3. If it promises high returns with little risk, stop.
    4. Report it to the OSC (1-877-785-1555) or the Canadian Anti-Fraud Centre.
    CSA National Registrant SearchCIRO AdvisorReport

    For you: Sentinel's kind of job: review a claim, never act on it.

    Watch out: CIRO says it will never ask for your banking details or ID copies; anyone who does while claiming to be a regulator is a fraudster.

  • TFSA, RRSP and FHSA in one line eachFrom the web

    TFSA: no deduction, but growth and withdrawals are tax-free. RRSP: contributions cut taxable income now; withdrawals are taxed later. FHSA: contributions are deductible, growth is untaxed, and qualifying withdrawals for a first home are tax-free.

    Watch out: Limits change each year; check your current room with the CRA, not with an AI.

    Fidelity Canada: TFSA, RRSP or FHSA web

    Checked 26 Oct 2026

  • What CIPF does and does not protectFrom the web

    The Canadian Investor Protection Fund returns your property if a member dealer goes insolvent, up to $1 million for general accounts (cash, margin, TFSA, FHSA), $1 million for retirement accounts (RRSP, RRIF, LIF), and $1 million for RESPs. Amounts in CAD. It does not cover market losses, bad advice, fraud, or crypto missing at insolvency. Claims must be filed within 180 days of the insolvency.

    Watch out: Losses from an AI bot or a scam are not covered; nor is a platform that is not a CIPF member.

    CIPF: About coverage web

    Checked 26 Oct 2026

  • Who regulates what: CIRO, the CSA and the OSCFrom the web

    The OSC regulates securities in Ontario and is one of the provincial members of the CSA, which runs SEDAR+ and the National Registrant Search. CIRO oversees investment dealers and keeps AdvisorReport. Before trusting any firm or app that touches your money, check it is registered.

Hermes agents, from zero to a team 10, in order

    The Hermes docs split learning into three tiers: Beginner (about 1 hour: install, quickstart, CLI, configuration), Intermediate (2 to 3 hours: sessions, messaging, tools, skills, memory, cron) and Advanced (4 to 6 hours: architecture, custom tools and skills). There is also a 'team of specialist Bots' route through Desktop, Profiles, Bot Mode and Cron.

    For you: The 'team of specialist Bots' route is the closest match to your seven-agent crew.

    Hermes docs: Learning Path web

    Sharbel A. and Metics Media both run the same zero-to-working path: host Hermes (your own machine, or a one-click Hostinger/Nous Portal VPS), connect a model, then connect Telegram so it reaches your phone. Alex Finn's desktop walkthrough covers the same ground.

    1. Host Hermes on a spare machine or a one-click VPS
    2. Connect a model in the dashboard and send a hello

    Hermes AgentHostinger VPSHermes desktop appTelegramOpenRouter
